stimulus.title: Precipitating barium sulfate
stimulus.text: To find the sulfate concentration in a 50.00 mL water sample, a student adds BaCl₂(aq) until no more white solid forms, then a few drops more. The solid, BaSO₄ (molar mass 233.40 g/mol), is filtered, rinsed, dried to constant mass and found to weigh 0.4668 g. The only sulfate compound in the water is Na₂SO₄.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate.

rubric.point: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s), with Na⁺ and Cl⁻ omitted.

parts.sample: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s). Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the molarity of sulfate ions in the water sample.

rubric.point: Moles BaSO₄ = 0.4668 g ÷ 233.40 g/mol = 0.002000 mol = moles SO₄²⁻ (1 : 1).

parts.sample: 0.4668 g BaSO₄ × (1 mol / 233.40 g) = 0.002000 mol BaSO₄, which came from 0.002000 mol SO₄²⁻ (1 : 1). Molarity = 0.002000 mol ÷ 0.05000 L = 0.04000 M sulfate.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The student skipped rinsing the precipitate, and some dissolved NaCl dried onto the solid. Predict the effect on the calculated sulfate molarity and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Too high, because the dried NaCl adds mass that is counted as BaSO₄, giving too many moles of sulfate.
accept: larger, since the extra salt is weighed as barium sulfate

parts.sample: Too high. The NaCl left on the solid adds to the weighed mass, which the calculation treats as BaSO₄. That gives too many moles of BaSO₄, and so of sulfate, and too large a molarity.
